explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” No hedging and no "well, some folks say." After a whole round of what other people think, he just says it plain.

Elijah, a prophet from long ago, was on the list, but that guess came from other people. The disciples said, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah…” Peter doesn't pick from that list at all. He answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Good guess, friend, because some people did name prophets. The disciples said, “and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” But Peter doesn't stop at prophet. He goes bigger: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Peter walks right past the crowd's answer.
That's right, friend. Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah!” Simon son of Jonah is Peter. He answers a big confession with a blessing, not a lecture.
Not quite, baker. Jesus answers Peter with, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah!” Simon son of Jonah is Peter. Jesus answers that big confession with a blessing.

That's the one. Jesus says, “For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.” So Peter's answer didn't come from his own figuring or from a crowd. I think that makes it a pretty special thing to say out loud.

An angel is a fair guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't name one here. He says this was not revealed to Peter by “…flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.” The answer Jesus gives is the Father. Angels show up all over the Bible, so I get the pick.

Andrew was Peter's brother, that part is true (Matthew 4:18). But Jesus says it was not revealed by “…flesh and blood…” and a brother is flesh and blood. Jesus names “…My Father in heaven.” Nice try, baker, but Andrew can't take this one.

Careful, friend, this one is flipped. Jesus says, “…I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” So the gates of Hades do not prevail. Read it slow and you can hear the confidence.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” The church He builds stays standing, and the gates of Hades don't win.

explanations.answer: It will be loosed in heaven
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus says, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” The two halves match up: bind with bound, loose with loosed. That's Jesus talking to Peter, right after promising him the keys.

explanations.answer: It will be bound in heaven
explanations.explanation: That's the first half you're thinking of, friend. Binding goes with “…bound in heaven…” Loosing goes with “…loosed in heaven.” The two halves of that sentence match each other, like two cookies in the same batch.

explanations.answer: It will be forgotten in heaven
explanations.explanation: Forgotten isn't a word in that sentence, baker. Jesus says, “…whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” He says loosed, not forgotten. Stick with His exact words and you can't go wrong.

Other way around, baker. The text says, “Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.” So no telling anyone for now. That's a surprising turn after Peter just said it out loud.
That's right, friend. Jesus “…admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.” He gives them the opposite of a megaphone. The text doesn't say why, so I'll leave that open too.

explanations.answer: He will be raised to life
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says He must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, “…and on the third day be raised to life.” The hard news and the good news come in the same sentence. Listen to the whole sentence, baker.
Galilee doesn't come up in this sentence, friend. Jesus says He must be killed “…and on the third day be raised to life.” The third day is about being raised, not about a trip.

explanations.answer: He will appear in the temple
explanations.explanation: No temple in this verse, baker. Jesus says that on the third day He will “…be raised to life.” That's the promise right there in the same breath as the suffering.

Yep. “Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him.” He says, “Far be it from You, Lord!” and “This shall never happen to You!” Right before that, Jesus had told His disciples He must suffer and be killed (Matthew 16:21). I think Peter's heart was in a big hurry, but the text just tells us what he said.
It really does say it, friend. “Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him.” Right after Jesus talks about suffering and being killed, Peter speaks up. He says, “This shall never happen to You!”

That's the word. Jesus says, “…you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.” It's a direct line to Peter. It comes right after “Get behind Me, Satan!” so Jesus is plain with him here.
Kings aren't in that sentence, baker. Jesus says, “…you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.” The contrast is God's things against men's things. No crowns needed.

Priests do show up earlier, because Jesus says in verse 21 that He will suffer at the hands of the “…elders, chief priests, and scribes…” But in this sentence He says, “…the things of God, but the things of men.” Good memory, friend, just a different spot.

That's it. Jesus says, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” Three things in a row: deny himself, take up his cross, follow. Jesus says this to His disciples after telling them what's ahead.
No staff in this verse, friend. Jesus says to “…deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” It's the cross He names.
Sword isn't in that sentence, baker. Jesus says, “…he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” The thing to take up is the cross, so put the sword back in the drawer.

Right, and it sounds backwards. Jesus says, “For whoever wants to save his life will lose it…” Holding on tight ends up costing the thing you were gripping. Then He turns it around in the second half of the verse.
That's the opposite of what Jesus says, friend. He says, “…whoever wants to save his life will lose it…” So the one who tries to save it is the one who loses it. It's a surprising line.

explanations.answer: He will win it back later
explanations.explanation: Close, but you've swapped the halves, baker. Finding it goes with the other person. Jesus says, “…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” The one who wants to save his life “…will lose it…”
Hold on, friend, the verse says the opposite. Jesus says, “…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” Find it, not lose it for good. Losing it for His sake ends with finding it.
That's right. Jesus says, “…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” So the one who loses it for His sake finds it. The other half of the verse is the one about losing.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?” He asks it as a question, and the answer is left for us to think about. Then He asks one more.
It's in there, friend. Jesus asks, “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?” The whole world is on one side of the scale and his soul is on the other.

explanations.answer: Repay each one for what he has done
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says the Son of Man “…will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done.” Notice that it's each one. I'm not here to tell you when, only to keep the ovens ready (Matthew 24:36).

explanations.answer: Gather only His disciples to Him
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse, baker. Jesus says, “…then He will repay each one according to what he has done.” It's each one, and the word “only” isn't there.
Jerusalem comes up a few verses earlier, but not a temple rebuild. In this verse, Jesus says the Son of Man “…will repay each one according to what he has done.” Stick to what He says, friend.

Read it again, baker. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.” So some of them will see it before they die. Not none.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “…some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.” So some of them will see it. He says it with “Truly I tell you…” and I don't try to say more than the verse does.
